The Guided Planet · Issue 001 · November 2026

Where every fact came from

Every fact in this issue, the source it came from, the words on that source that back it up, and anything a careful reader should know about it.

  1. ESA Education and the Raspberry Pi Foundation, Mission Zero

    Checked 2026-10-13. Official programme page. Used on page 3.

    What it supports: What Mission Zero is: a Python program showing an image on an Astro Pi on the ISS, using the colour sensor for the background; browser based, no hardware or prior skills; certificate showing the ISS position.

    You will write a Python program to display a personalised image (or animation) on an Astro Pi computer on board the ISS. No special hardware or prior coding skills needed.

  2. ESA Education and the Raspberry Pi Foundation, Mission Zero guidelines

    Checked 2026-10-13. Official programme page. Used on page 3.

    What it supports: The 30 second limit, no surnames, the 22 March 2027 deadline.

    Your program must not run for longer than 30 seconds. Please do not include team members' surnames. The deadline for submitting entries to Mission Zero is 12:00 noon CET on 22 March 2027.

  3. ESA Education and the Raspberry Pi Foundation, Mission Zero eligibility

    Checked 2026-10-13. Official programme page. Used on page 3.

    What it supports: Aged 19 or younger at submission, at a school, club or registered home school in an eligible country including the UK; teams up to 4; a mentor such as a teacher or parent.

    Aged 19 or younger at the time of submission. Working individually or in a team of up to 4 young people. Supervised by a mentor such as a teacher, educator, parent...

    Worth knowing: A general Astro Pi rule asks that at least half of a team are nationals of an ESA member state, so the paper says who can enter without saying 'anyone'.

  4. Raspberry Pi Foundation, An astronomical anniversary: young people's code heads to the International Space Station

    Published 22 April 2026. Checked 2026-10-13. Press release. Used on page 3.

    What it supports: 2025/26 season: 24,695 young people took part in Mission Zero (17,381 submissions); 25,707 young people across both missions were due to have programs run in space.

    17,381 submissions for Mission Zero from 24,695 young explorers... In total, 25,707 young people will have their programs run in space

    Worth knowing: Organiser's own count. 25,707 was written before the programs ran, so the paper says 'were due to'.

  5. Raspberry Pi Foundation, Launching Astro Pi 2026/27: code your way to the International Space Station

    Published 14 September 2026. Checked 2026-10-13. Press release. Used on page 3.

    What it supports: Mission Zero is ideal for young people aged 9 to 16 with no prior coding experience.

    perfect for young people aged 9 to 16 with no prior coding experience

  6. Raspberry Pi, Sense HAT

    Checked 2026-10-13. Official programme page. Used on page 3.

    What it supports: The Sense HAT has an 8 by 8 RGB LED matrix and was developed for the ISS.

    The bright 8×8 RGB LED matrix allows you to visualise data from the sensors... The Sense HAT was originally developed for use on the International Space Station

    Worth knowing: The 2026/27 Mission Zero pages do not mention the matrix size, so the paper says the Sense HAT has the grid and that Mission Zero code is planned on it, not that every flight unit is a Sense HAT.

  13. Sanders, Noetel, Parker and colleagues, Nature Human Behaviour, An umbrella review of the benefits and risks associated with youths' interactions with electronic screens

    Published 2024. Checked 2026-10-13. Systematic review. Used on page 6.

    What it supports: 102 meta-analyses (2,451 studies, about 1.9 million participants); small to moderate associations that depend on the type of screen use; literacy negatively associated overall but positive with parental co-viewing.

    screen use was negatively associated with literacy (r = -0.14) but this effect was positive when parents watched with their children (r = 0.15)... carefully weigh the evidence for potential harms and benefits of specific types of screen use

    Worth knowing: Associations, mostly from correlational studies; 95 of 102 meta-analyses at medium to high risk of bias.

  14. Kaye, Orben, Ellis, Hunter and Houghton, IJERPH, The Conceptual and Methodological Mayhem of 'Screen Time'

    Published 2020. Checked 2026-10-13. Peer reviewed study. Used on page 6.

    What it supports: Findings are mixed and lack causal evidence; measures are mostly self report.

    Existing research presents mixed findings, and lacks longitudinal evidence for any causal or long-term effects... the use of non-standardised measures that are predominantly self-report

  15. Valkenburg, van Driel and Beyens, New Media and Society, The associations of active and passive social media use with well-being: A critical scoping review

    Published 2022. Checked 2026-10-13. Systematic review. Used on page 6.

    What it supports: Across 40 studies, most did not support the hypothesised active good, passive bad associations.

    Most studies did not support the hypothesized associations of ASMU and PSMU with well-/ill-being.

    Worth knowing: Of the studies reviewed, most were of adults and only a minority of (pre)adolescents, so it does not speak for 7 to 12 year olds.

  16. Yau, Reich and Lee, Journal of Adolescent Health, Coping With Stress Through Texting: An Experimental Study

    Published 2021. Checked 2026-10-13. Peer reviewed study. Used on page 7.

    What it supports: 130 adolescents, mean age 12.41; texting a friend after a stressor gave higher mood than no activity or watching a video.

    Participants who texted their friend reported higher moods... than those in the no activity condition... and higher moods than adolescents in the passive-phone condition.

    Worth knowing: One lab session with a friend the young person already texted regularly. Mood was higher than both comparison groups; stress was lower only than the sit quietly group. Mean age 12.4.

  17. UNICEF Innocenti, Responsible Innovation in Technology for Children (RITEC), phase 2 report

    Published April 2024. Checked 2026-10-13. Official report. Used on page 7.

    What it supports: Digital games can contribute to children's wellbeing, including relationships, and different games support different aspects depending on design; samples included children aged 8 to 12.

    digital games can indeed contribute to the well-being of children... not all games are equal: different games support different aspects of well-being depending on how they are designed.

    Worth knowing: Co-founded with the LEGO Group and funded by the LEGO Foundation. Mixed methods, small samples.
